newsitem.title: PERU: Japan runs scaled-down embassy in Peru after siege.
newsitem.headline: Japan runs scaled-down embassy in Peru after siege.

text.p: How do you run a Japanese embassy when the ambassador and most of the diplomats are held hostage by 20 heavily armed Marxist rebels?
The first thing you do is to stop issuing visas.

The siege of ambassador Morihisa Aoki's residence by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels has created a logistical nightmare for Japanese officials trying to conduct "business as usual" while managing the hostage crisis that has now dragged into its 10th day.
A 50-member diplomatic "task force" rushed to Lima, led by Japan's ambassador to Mexico Terusuke Terada, was made up of officials from Tokyo, Latin America and the United States.

Not all of them speak Spanish. And there is no way for them to pose questions to their besieged colleagues inside the fortified residence that the guerrillas stormed during a lavish cocktail party last Tuesday.

"We're just charging on," one senior official said. "Anybody who knows anything is inside" -- including those authorised to sign the visas for entry to Japan or contracts from Japan's massive Overseas Development Aid (ODA) to Peru.
Pablo Sanchez, a carpenter who said his employer was performing construction work for the Japanese embassy, said: "I haven't been given my Christmas bonus -- they have not signed the check."
Japan said on Thursday it would stop issuing visas for Peruvians travelling to Japan.
"There are only a couple of officials who can stamp those visas, and we can't really transfer that authority to someone else at this point," a task force official said.
Peruvians, many of whom travel to Japan as manual workers, sometimes illegally, will just have to get on a plane and apply for admittance at the airport upon arrival in Japan, he said.

The Peruvian-Japanese Society in Lima said it had not received any complaints yet from Peruvians unable to get visas for Japan. "I think everyone understands that this is something they will have to live with for a while," a Society spokeswoman said.

Other diplomatic activities were continuing with skeleton staff, task force officials said. Most communication equipment including devices to send coded messages were still safely inside the embassy, they added.
The embassy itself is in the district of Jesus Maria, about one mile (two km) from the ambassador's residence, and was staying open.
The task force, meanwhile, has ended up spending most of the past week dealing with a barrage of media inquiries from the hordes of journalists who have descended on Lima.

Japanese media, frustrated by the tight-lipped government and its guarded briefings, have begun a campaign of "exclusives." The speculation has ranged from a deal struck with Cuba to the discovery of a Japanese-speaking female MRTA spy infiltrating the task force.
Both were denied by the officials in Lima.

The task force has also had to keep track of the hundreds of released hostages. The officials also scoured Japanese restaurants in the city to order special lunch boxes, called bento, to send to the hostages for their Christmas meal.

"It's only been a week since we started up here, so we're taking it one day at a time," said one senior task force official. "Our purpose is to promote a peaceful solution to the crisis and to help preserve lives. But frankly, I haven't really thought about the serious stuff much."
